list.listitem: Moderate to severe onychocryptosis (ingrown toenail).
Failed topical and oral treatment of onychomycosis (fungal infection of the toenail).
Recurrent or chronic paronychia.
Patients should be referred if sensitivity to anesthetics, potential for bleeding complications, or vascular medical problems (i.e. peripheral vascular occlusive disease).
Recommendations based largely on expert opinion since clinical trials are lacking.

Obtain surgical consent after risks, benefits and alternatives have been appropriately explained. Place the patient in a supine or seated position with the affected toe and foot in a position comfortable for the provider (resting or hanging off the end of the table).
Swab the affected toe with povidone iodine solution.

Use 6 to 8 ml of 1% or 2% lidocaine or bupivicaine (without epinephrine) for local anesthesia in a digital block fashion. Insert a 25- to 30-gauge needle inch into the 1st digit webspace and inject 1 to 2 ml of anesthetic. Insert the needle perpendicular to the bone at the base of the great toe until bone is reached. Pull back 1 to 2 mm and inject 1 ml into the lateral aspect and 1 ml across the dorsal and ventral surfaces in the subcutaneous space. Repeat on the contralateral side.
Use a tourniquet or rubber band around the toe to assist in hemostasis for shortest duration necessary (usually less than 5 minutes); use with caution in patients with diabetes mellitus.
Identify the lateral 20% to 25% of the ingrown nail as the site of the partial lateral nail avulsion. Use a nail elevator under the nail to separate it from the nail bed.
Use a nail splitter to cut from the distal end of the toenail straight back toward the cuticle beneath the nail fold.

Grasp the avulsed lateral nail fragment with a hemostat down to just past the cuticle. Remove it by twisting the avulsed nail outward toward the lateral nail fold while pulling in straight direction toward the end of the toe. Ensure that the entire nail fragment and flat edge of the nail bed is retrieved to prevent formation of a nail spicule and the potential for recurrence of an ingrown nail.

Release the tourniquet after adequate hemostasis is achieved. Several options for destruction of the nail-forming matrix beneath where the nail plate was removed include: Phenolization: Apply an 80% to 88% phenol solution directly to the nail matrix 3 times for 30 seconds each round, then thoroughly cleanse with 70% isopropyl alcohol to neutralize the phenol. Apply phenol with a Q-tip only to the matrix and not the nail bed or surrounding tissues, which may delay wound healing. Phenol should not be used if the patient, physician, or medical assistants are pregnant (pregnancy risk category: C) Phenol plus simple avulsion reduces the risk of recurrence compared with simple avulsion alone (OR 0.07; 95% CI 0.04-0.12) and compared with more complex surgical excisions (OR 0.44; 95% CI 0.24-0.80). However, use of phenol also significantly increases the risk of post-operative infection (OR 5.7; 95% CI 1.9-17). A subsequent systematic review of 18 studies with 1655 concluded that for every 1000 patients treated there are 175 fewer cases of discharge or hemorrhage, 257 fewer patients with significant pain, and 49 fewer recurrences. After phenolization, irrigation with alcohol plus chlorhexidine is more effective for removing residual phenol compared to alcohol alone; both solutions are equally effective with multiple irrigations. Electrocautery, radiofrequency or CO2 laser ablation of the nail matrix may also be used for removal of any adjacent granulation tissue, but these methods have been shown to be less effective than phenolization in preventing reoccurrence. Direct surgical excision of the partial nail matrix was shown to be similar in effectiveness (i.e. recurrence and infection) to phenol in one small RCT with 63 patients.
After surgery, apply a dressing of bacitracin/polymixin ointment, 4 × 4 gauze, tube gauze, and paper tape, ensuring a comfortable bandage (variations on materials are acceptable).

After 24 to 48 hours, soak the affected toe in a warm soapy bath and reapply bacitracin/polymixin ointment with a clean bandage. This should be done 3 to 4 times daily for 1 to 2 weeks after the procedure.

Oral antibiotics are not recommended unless there are signs of cellulitis or soft tissue infection. There is also no evidence showing that pretreatment with antibiotics before surgery improves outcomes.
Incomplete matricectomy can result in a regrowth of a nail spicule along the new lateral nail fold. This new nail growth results in an inflammatory reaction, often necessitating another procedure.
If infection of the lateral nail fold is suspected, an oral antibiotic should be prescribed that covers common skin flora (e.g. cephalexin 500 mg orally four times daily for 5-7 days).

Overaggressive electrocautery or radiofrequency ablation to the nail matrix may damage the adjacent and underlying fascia or periosteum. If the toe is healing poorly several weeks after the procedure, debridement, oral antibiotics and radiographic evaluation may be warranted.
No routine follow-up is needed.
